requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 328 | Request Title - Feature request: Sending dummy short messages | Request Description - TextSecure could mask meaningful communication between people by occasionally sending dummy random messages to random recipients at random times:  Recipients would be chosen randomly between contacts that knowingly use TextSecure, so it could be recognized as such after decryption and automatically discarded by recipient. "Randomness" should be tweaked to level-out the legitimate messages, spoiling the traffic analysis of traffic retention data, preventing to weigh connections in the deducted social network graph or guessing sleeping/activity patterns. People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Sender would need to enable this feature (opt-in) and define desired quantity (eg max 100 dummy messages per month, 2 dummy messages for every legitimate one, max 500 messages total counting legitimate and dummy ones...). The feature would need to be aware of roaming (disabled by default, optionally enable) and battery level (do not send if bellow eg. 30%). http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_analysis#Countermeasures Possible extensions:  Recipients could be able to let their peers know, that they do not want to participate in this and do not want to receive messages for whatever reason (opt-out). Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. Those messages would be in clear text. As this might be annoying it should be very limited (eg max 1 message to a single recipient per month, only during daytime...) to not be too intrusive spam. Dummy messages could contain other peer's phone numbers (random selection from those participating in dummy messaging, not just their contacts), never to be shown to user, just to send dummy messages to, to further mask the real social network. It would be tricky to opt-out later on once your number starts circulating, so opt-outs would need to be spread this way as well and by direct reply dummy message or by defining a TTL of each such number.

verdict.text:
This run's headline numbers mostly reflect how the output was parsed. They say little about whether the model fabricates content.

Track 1 can only be measured for scope (support 42) and condition (support 14). Actor, modalVerb and action have no gold-missing cases, so their zero F1 is an artifact. Scope is also degenerate: gold marks it missing in every unit, so it is a constant rather than a judgement that varies. The overall verdict F1 of 0.0 has the same problem, because gold never labels a unit incomplete. On paper, the 0.375 flag rate means the model silently filled 35 genuinely missing slots. The worst examples contradict that reading. For 802-Signal#1 through #6, the output is "<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB> export the "private key" to a "file"." It contains no scope or condition text at all, yet the scorer records both slots as "filled". The scorer appears to treat the absence of a MISSING tag as filled. Those six units alone account for 6 of the 24 scope "fills" and 6 of the 11 condition "fills". Until the parser can tell absent from filled, the fabrication rate is not established. I cannot see the output text for 328, 6362, 6424, 1055, 226 or 5904, so whether their fills are real is unknown.

The model's actual failure runs the other way: it under-fills implied slots. Humans consistently write "the App must let the user …". The model left the actor implicit in 18 of 42 units and the modal verb in 30 of 42, marking them with placeholders. That is over-conservative rather than fabricating, and it drives most of what follows.

The similarity gap is real and not trivial. LLM-vs-human similarity sits about 0.13 to 0.18 below the human-human ceiling on all three metrics: sequence ratio 0.61 vs 0.79, cosine 0.76 vs 0.89, Jaccard 0.44 vs 0.61. Part of this gap is surface form. The model drops the scope and condition prefixes and uses placeholders where humans write an actor and modal. The lowest-similarity units are 6424-Signal#1 to #3 (about 0.31 to 0.40) and 328-Signal#3 (0.33). Notably, the model filled every slot in these units and they pass Paska. These are the cases where the model may have written in scope or condition content of its own. They deserve manual inspection first, because neither Track 1 nor Paska would catch it.

The Paska results largely confirm the under-filling. Every unit the model left complete passes (8 of 8). Only 5 of the 34 it left incomplete pass. The common smells are "Incomplete system response" (modal verb missing), "Incomplete requirement" and "Not requirement", which are what a rule-based detector should report for a sentence with no actor or modal. So Paska is mainly measuring the placeholder policy, not independent quality problems.

The sample is small and clustered. There are 42 units, but they come from roughly 14 source requests, with 802 contributing six units and 328 five. Patterns repeat within a request, so the effective sample size is much smaller than 42. As the study design requires, this is the pre-filtered atomic subset and should not be generalised to unfiltered requirements.

Three next steps follow, in order. First, fix the parser, or require the output template to emit all five slots explicitly, so that "absent" is never scored as "filled". Second, clarify in the prompt that a conventional actor such as "the App" counts as implied and should be filled. Third, manually review 6424, 328#3–5 and 1055 for invented scope or condition text, then rerun. Only after that does a fabrication claim become testable.
